title: Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning
venue: STATED IN THE VENDORED TEXT: '31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017), Long Beach, CA, USA.' [line 54, the footnote on the first page]. Unlike ewc.json, the venue is printed in the file and may be cited to it.
axis_note: Theta-path, but a THIRD kind of Theta-path that the S0 taxonomy did not anticipate. EWC (1612.00796) protects the past by adding a data-free penalty to the objective; generative replay (1705.08690) protects the past by regenerating data and putting it back into calR_k. GEM does neither: it keeps raw past examples in a trainer-side buffer, never trains on them, and instead uses them only to compute reference gradients that CONSTRAIN THE DIRECTION of the current update. The objective is untouched; the feasible set of updates is what changes. In frame terms GEM is (U-Theta) with a projection operator applied to the gradient, not with a modified calL. There is no W anywhere (nothing moves at answer time), and the episodic memory is NOT an external store E in the §1.6 sense: ret(E,q) is never invoked, no retrieved content ever enters a forward pass at query time, and the deployed artifact after the last task is one ordinary weight vector (plus per-task linear heads on CIFAR-100). Calling GEM an 'E-path' method because it stores examples would be a defect; the store is consumed by the optimiser, exactly like EWC's Atari replay buffers.

problem_stated.statement: Standard supervised learning assumes iid samples from one fixed distribution and multiple passes over a training set; humans instead see an ordered stream, rarely see the same example twice, can memorise only a few pieces of data, and the stream spans different tasks. 'In fact, straightforward applications of ERM lead to "catastrophic forgetting" [McCloskey and Cohen, 1989]. That is, the learner forgets how to solve past tasks after it is exposed to new tasks.' [lines 36-41]
problem_stated.the_object_of_study: A CONTINUUM OF DATA: '(x_1, t_1, y_1), ..., (x_i, t_i, y_i), ..., (x_n, t_n, y_n)' [Eq. (1), line 44], where t_i is a TASK DESCRIPTOR. 'Importantly, examples are not drawn iid from a fixed probability distribution over triplets (x, t, y), since a whole sequence of examples from the current task may be observed before switching to the next task.' [lines 49-51]. The only structural assumption retained is local iid-ness: 'we assume that the continuum is locally iid, that is, every triplet (x_i, t_i, y_i) satisfies (x_i, y_i) ~iid P_{t_i}(X, Y).' [lines 77-80]
problem_stated.three_named_challenges: 1. Non-iid input data; 2. Catastrophic forgetting; 3. Transfer learning -- 'when the tasks in the continuum are related, there exists an opportunity for transfer learning. This would translate into faster learning of new tasks, as well as performance improvements in old tasks.' [lines 56-63]
problem_stated.the_evaluation_complaint_that_motivates_: 'Most of the literature about learning over a sequence of tasks [Rusu et al., 2016, Fernando et al., 2017, Kirkpatrick et al., 2017, Rebuffi et al., 2017] describes a setting where i) the number of tasks is small, ii) the number of examples per task is large, iii) the learner performs several passes over the examples concerning each task, and iv) the only metric reported is the average performance across all tasks. In contrast, we are interested in the "more human-like" setting where i) the number of tasks is large, ii) the number of training examples per task is small, iii) the learner observes the examples concerning each task only once, and iv) we report metrics that measure both transfer and forgetting.' [lines 98-104]
problem_stated.why_this_matters_for_the_monograph: This is the paper that supplies the corpus with its MEASUREMENT LANGUAGE for forgetting. Every later claim in the Theta path that says 'we forget less' is, directly or indirectly, a BWT claim in GEM's sense. The frame's rho has no other operational definition anywhere in this corpus.

inherited_open_question.verdict: inherited-implicitly-from-EWC, and stated as a LIMITATION of EWC rather than as a quotation of EWC's own open question
inherited_open_question.detail: GEM quotes no prior paper's stated open question verbatim. Its bridge-in is a two-part complaint against the state of the art it names -- [Kirkpatrick et al., 2017] (= EWC) and [Rebuffi et al., 2017] (= iCaRL).
inherited_open_question.part_1_the_protocol_complaint: EWC and iCaRL are charged with evaluating in a regime that is too easy and too coarse: few tasks, many examples per task, multiple passes, and only average accuracy reported [lines 98-104]. GEM's answer is the (K=20 tasks, 1000 or 2500 examples per task, single pass) protocol plus the three metrics ACC/BWT/FWT [Eqs. (2)-(4)].
inherited_open_question.part_2_the_mechanism_complaint: The decisive inherited limitation is that BOTH prior families forbid positive backward transfer. Of the loss-on-memory option: 'Obviously, minimizing the loss at the current example together with (5) results in overfitting to the examples stored in M_k. As an alternative, we could keep the predictions at past tasks invariant by means of distillation [Rebuffi et al., 2017]. However, this would deem positive backward transfer impossible. Instead, we will use the losses (5) as inequality constraints, avoiding their increase but allowing their decrease.' [lines 194-198]. And explicitly against EWC: 'In contrast to the state-of-the-art [Kirkpatrick et al., 2017, Rebuffi et al., 2017], our model therefore allows positive backward transfer.' [lines 200-201]
inherited_open_question.what_EWC_actually_left_open_that_this_an: EWC's memory of a past task is a Gaussian centred on the OLD SOLUTION [ewc, §2 lines 137-146], so any movement away from Theta*_{k-1} is penalised regardless of whether it helps or hurts the old task. EWC never asks whether the penalty could be made one-sided. GEM's whole mechanism is that question answered: replace the two-sided quadratic well by a one-sided inequality on the past loss, so downhill motion on old tasks is free and only uphill motion is blocked.
inherited_open_question.restated_for_the_bridge_chain: EWC compresses the past into a SHAPE (a quadratic well). Generative replay compresses the past into a SAMPLER. GEM refuses to compress at all -- it keeps a small raw sample and spends it on a DIRECTION TEST. The three are the three ways a Theta-path system can carry calH_{<k} forward, and ch07 is where the corpus first has all three in hand.

core_mechanism.one_line: Keep m raw examples per past task; at every optimiser step compute the current gradient g and one reference gradient g_k per past task; if any inner product <g, g_k> is negative, replace g by the nearest gradient (in squared L2) whose inner products with all g_k are non-negative, obtained by solving a QP whose dual has only (k-1) variables.
core_mechanism.in_frame_words: Canonical (U-Theta) is Theta_{k+1} = Theta_k - eta_Theta grad_Theta calL(calR_k; Theta_k) with calR_k = gen(calH_k; B_s). GEM keeps calR_k = the CURRENT task's stream (like EWC, the history is not trained on) and keeps calL unchanged (unlike EWC, which adds a penalty term). The history re-enters through a PROJECTION applied to the gradient before the step: grad -> Pi_feasible(grad). There is no sleep round at all -- the projection is paid at every single optimiser step, inside the wake-time training loop.

core_mechanism.reduction_to_frame: GEM = (U-Theta) with the gradient replaced by its projection onto a feasible cone defined by stored past gradients. calL is UNCHANGED (contrast EWC, which changes calL). calR_k is the current task's stream only (same as EWC). gen(calH_k; B_s) is not a generator at all: a fixed-size subsample of calH_{<k} is retained verbatim (last m examples per task) and is used only as a source of constraint directions. B_s in the frame's sense is zero -- there is NO offline round -- and the entire consolidation cost is paid inline, at every optimiser step. Read side: equation (R) collapses to y-hat = f(q; Theta) on MNIST, and to y-hat = f(q, k; Theta) on CIFAR-100, where the task descriptor selects one of K per-task linear heads [§4.2, lines 341-343]. W is empty; ret(E,q) is never called.

three_way_contrast_for_ch07.the_sentence_ch07_should_carry: EWC changes what you are optimising. Replay changes what you are optimising it on. GEM changes neither, and instead changes which directions you are allowed to move in. Only the third one is one-sided, and one-sidedness is exactly what buys positive backward transfer.

outer_vs_inner.readers_first_answer: Everything GEM learns, it learns by ordinary SGD while streaming. The only thing that distinguishes a GEM step from an SGD step is that the gradient is filtered before it is applied. At answer time GEM is indistinguishable from any other network of the same architecture -- the same forward pass, the same weights, no retrieval, no adaptation. All of GEM's machinery lives in the optimiser.
outer_vs_inner.which_is_the_sleep_round: THERE IS NONE. This is the single most important structural fact about GEM for this monograph. EWC at least concentrates its consolidation work at the task boundary (snapshot + Fisher). GEM distributes it uniformly over every optimiser step: k-1 extra backward passes and one small QP, per mini-batch of 10 examples. In the frame's vocabulary, GEM has B_s = 0 and a permanently inflated wake-time training cost. Any ch07 sentence that calls GEM a 'sleep' or 'consolidation phase' method is a defect.

update_layer.instantiates: (U-Theta) ONLY, with a projection operator inserted between the gradient and the step.
not_instantiated: (U-W): absent. No fast-weight state, no per-token or per-chunk update, no retention gate alpha_t, no momentum/surprise S_t. Read equation (R) collapses to y-hat = f(q; Theta) (MNIST) or f(q, k; Theta) (CIFAR).

(U-E): absent BY THE §1.6 TEST, despite the paper's word 'memory'. The episodic memory E^{tr} is written during training and read by the optimiser; it is never read by ret(E,q) and never enters a forward pass at answer time. The distinction matters because GEM is frequently mis-shelved as a retrieval method. It is not: a deployed GEM model can throw the memory away.
difference_from_canonical: calL is untouched. This is the exact inverse of EWC, whose entire mechanism is an added term in calL. Two Theta-path papers, adjacent in the same year, intervene at two different places in the same update rule.

gen(calH_k; B_s) is replaced by a fixed-size verbatim retention window (last m per task), and its product is consumed as CONSTRAINT DIRECTIONS rather than as training data. The paper is explicit that consuming it as training data would be wrong: 'minimizing the loss at the current example together with (5) results in overfitting to the examples stored in M_k' [lines 194-195].
The step is Theta <- Theta - eta_Theta * Proj(grad), not Theta <- Theta - eta_Theta * grad. Proj is the Euclidean projection onto {u : <u, g_j> >= 0 for all j < k}, computed by the dual QP (gem-11).

The per-step cost scales with the ROUND INDEX: at round k there are k-1 extra backward passes. Canonical (U-Theta) has per-step cost independent of k. This is the property that decides whether GEM survives to LLM scale (it does not, in this form -- see systems_implications).
eta_Theta is not modulated. GEM never adjusts a learning rate; it rotates and rescales the direction. Contrast the effective-learning-rate rhetoric EWC uses about its own penalty.
update_layer.order_within_a_round: (1) observe (x, k, y); (2) append (x, y) to E^{tr}_k; (3) g <- grad of the current loss; (4) for each j < k, g_j <- grad of the memory loss (gem-6) -- k-1 backward passes; (5) if any <g, g_j> < 0, solve the (k-1)-variable dual QP (gem-11), add gamma to v*, set g-tilde = G^T v* + g; else g-tilde = g; (6) Theta <- Theta - eta_Theta g-tilde. Steps 3-5 repeat for EVERY mini-batch of 10 examples. (7) At the end of round k only: run EVALUATE on all K test partitions and write row Pi_{k,:}.
update_layer.gating: None. Unlike EWC's Atari 20M-frame gate, GEM's constraints become active as soon as there is at least one past task -- i.e. from the first example of round 2.

cost_table.note_on_units: GEM is a 2017 training-time algorithm with no notion of a query, a session, or a user, and -- unlike the rest of this corpus -- with no offline phase at all. Two of the four cells are therefore absent. Where the paper does report cost, it reports it in wall-clock CPU seconds and in memory SLOTS, never in FLOPs or bytes. Nothing below is estimated; arithmetic performed by this note is labelled as such.

B_s.why: The frame defines B_s as compute spent BEFORE a query arrives, in an idle period. GEM has no such period. Its consolidation cost is paid inside the training loop at every optimiser step, so there is no quantity in the paper that B_s could name. This is a structural absence, not an omission.
B_s.what_is_measured_instead: Total CPU training time for the whole 20-task MNIST continuum, Table 1 [caption line 475, values lines 476-505], in seconds: permutations -- single 11, independent 11, multimodal 14, EWC 179, GEM 77; rotations -- single 11, independent 16, multimodal 13, EWC 169, GEM 135. GEM is 7.0x (perm) and 12.3x (rot) the cost of the unregularised 'single' baseline, and 0.43x (perm) / 0.80x (rot) the cost of the paper's EWC implementation. The ratios are this note's arithmetic on the paper's printed integers.
B_s.what_the_paper_claims_from_it: 'Overall, GEM performs significantly better than other continual learning methods like EWC, while spending less computation (Table 1). GEM's efficiency comes from optimizing over a number of variables equal to the number of tasks (T = 20 in our experiments), instead of optimizing over a number of variables equal to the number of parameters (p = 1109240 for CIFAR100 for instance). GEM's bottleneck is the necessity of computing previous task gradients at each learning iteration.' [§4.4, lines 595-599]
B_s.what_is_absent: No FLOPs. No GPU time (Table 1 is CPU only). NO CIFAR-100 TIMING AT ALL -- the table covers MNIST only, and CIFAR is where |Theta| = 1109240 makes the k-1 backward passes most expensive. No per-step breakdown between the gradient passes and the QP solve. No wall-clock for the QP. No energy.

L_w.detail: No latency, TTFT, throughput, ms/example or ms/token figure appears anywhere. Structurally the answer-time cost is exactly the unmodified network's forward pass: Algorithm 1's EVALUATE procedure [lines 284-294] takes no gradient, consults no memory, and writes no state. On CIFAR-100 the only answer-time addition is head selection by the task descriptor [§4.2, lines 341-343], whose cost is a single linear layer and is never measured.
L_w.source: absence across the paper; Algorithm 1 lines 284-294; §4.2 lines 341-343

C_cap.stated_budget: 'the learner has a total budget of M memory locations. If the number of total tasks T is known, we can allocate m = M/T memories for each task.' [§3, lines 179-181]. The selected budget for every GEM run is 5120: 'memory size: [5120 (rot, perm, cifar)]' [App. A, line 804]. With K = 20 that is m = 256 examples per task (arithmetic by this note).

GEM outperforms iCARL for a wide range of memory sizes.' [lines 606-608]. Note that monotone increase over the whole sweep means the curve has NOT saturated at 5120 -- the reported operating point is the largest one tried.
C_cap.as_a_fraction_of_the_stream: MNIST: 20 tasks x 1000 examples = 20,000 examples in the stream, of which 5,120 are retained verbatim = 25.6%. CIFAR-100: 20 x 2500 = 50,000, of which 5,120 = 10.24%. Both fractions are this note's arithmetic on §4.1 lines 331-333 and App. A line 804; NEITHER APPEARS IN THE PAPER. ch07 must state them: GEM is a large-footprint rehearsal method wearing a constraint-method's clothes.
C_cap.transient_state: G in R^{(k-1) x |Theta|} must exist at every step. On CIFAR-100 with |Theta| = 1109240 [line 598] and k-1 = 19 that is 21,075,560 floats = 84.3 MB in fp32 (arithmetic by this note). The paper never mentions this cost.

On the other hand, memory-based methods such as EWC and GEM lead to higher ACC as the number of passes through the data increases.' [lines 609-616]
rho.the_finding_for_the_monograph: rho is not a property of a method alone; it is a property of (method x how hard you train on the new round). More optimisation on the new task buys more forgetting, and the memory-free methods pay for it monotonically. This is the sharpest statement of the sleep-round sustainability problem anywhere in the corpus, and it comes from a 2017 MNIST table.

scale_ceiling.what_the_ceiling_forbids: Any claim in this monograph that GEM-style constraint projection is practical at LLM scale. The mechanism requires K-1 full gradients of |Theta| resident simultaneously; at |Theta| = 1109240 that is 84.3 MB in fp32 and invisible, but the same construction at 7B parameters and 19 tasks is 19 x 14 GB = 266 GB in bf16 (arithmetic by this note, not in the paper). GEM's cost argument -- 'a QP on t-1 << p variables' -- is about the QP, and the QP was never the expensive part.
scale_ceiling.single_run_caveat: Every number in the paper is from ONE run. No seeds, no error bars, no confidence intervals, no repetition, anywhere in the main text or the appendices.

extended_or_renamed.detail: GEM's §5 supplies the corpus's cleanest two-way naming: '"synaptic" memory [Kirkpatrick et al., 2017, Zenke et al., 2017], where learning rates are adjusted to minimize changes in parameters important for previous tasks' versus '"episodic" memory [Jung et al., 2016, Li and Hoiem, 2016, Rannen Triki et al., 2017, Rebuffi et al., 2017], where examples from previous tasks are stored and replayed to maintain predictions invariant by means of distillation' [lines 651-657]. GEM then places itself in the second family while rejecting its mechanism.
'Large negative backward transfer is also known as (catastrophic) forgetting.' [lines 116-117] -- the qualitative phenomenon becomes a signed scalar.

retired_or_demoted.reason: GEM's §2 argues it hides both transfer directions [lines 98-104]. After this paper, an ACC-only continual-learning result is incomplete by the field's own standard.

retired_or_demoted.concept: the assumption that protecting the past necessarily costs the past's improvability
retired_or_demoted.reason: shown false by construction: a one-sided constraint protects without freezing [lines 196-201].

open_questions.question: How should structured task descriptors be exploited to obtain positive FORWARD transfer (zero-shot learning)?
open_questions.verbatim: 'GEM does not leverage structured task descriptors, which may be exploited to obtain positive forward transfer (zero-shot learning).' [§6, lines 679-680]. Foreshadowed at lines 87-95 ('task descriptors t_i could be structured objects, such as a paragraph of natural language') and conceded at lines 175-178 ('When using integer task descriptors, one cannot expect significant positive forward transfer (zero-shot learning)').
open_questions.who_takes_it_up_in_this_corpus: Nobody in the Theta path. The descriptor-as-natural-language idea is picked up, unwittingly, by the E path a decade later: a 'paragraph of natural language explaining how to solve the i-th task' is precisely what ReasoningBank (2509.25140) stores and what MemGPT (2310.08560) pages in. ch07's bridge-out should name this as a dormant question that the E path answers without citing it.

open_questions.question: What is the right memory management policy? The paper uses the crudest possible one.
open_questions.verbatim: 'we did not investigate advanced memory management (such as building coresets of tasks [Lucic et al., 2017]).' [§6, lines 680-681]; and at the point of definition, 'we assume that the memory is populated with the last m examples from each task, although better memory update strategies could be employed (such as building a coreset per task).' [lines 182-184]

open_questions.question: How do you avoid paying one backward pass per past task at every single step?
open_questions.verbatim: 'each GEM iteration requires one backward pass per task, increasing computation time.' [§6, lines 682-683]; 'GEM's bottleneck is the necessity of computing previous task gradients at each learning iteration.' [§4.4, line 599]
open_questions.why_it_matters_here: This is the question that decides GEM's fate at scale, and it is the one the paper leaves in the weakest state -- it is stated as a fact, with no proposal. In the frame's terms: GEM has no B_s to amortise the cost into, so the cost has nowhere to go but into wake-time training.

unfavorable_facts.severity: high for this monograph's cost framing
unfavorable_facts.claim: GEM retains a large fraction of the raw stream verbatim, and the paper never says so. M = 5120 of 20,000 MNIST examples = 25.6%; 5120 of 50,000 CIFAR examples = 10.24% (arithmetic by this note from §4.1 lines 331-333 and App. A line 804). GEM is therefore a heavy rehearsal method by storage, even though its mechanism is not rehearsal. This is exactly the capacity objection EWC raised against replay -- 'it would require the amount of memories being stored and replayed to be proportional to the number of tasks' [ewc §1 lines 50-54] -- and GEM does not answer it; it accepts it and fixes the budget by hand.

The memory-size ablation exists only on CIFAR-100. On both MNIST datasets GEM is run at a single budget (5120) with no sweep [App. A line 804], so the paper's MNIST headline numbers -- its strongest results, including the +0.0247 positive BWT on permutations -- have no capacity ablation behind them. Table 2 also stops at the largest grid point without saturating.

The cost table (Table 1) covers MNIST only and is CPU-only. The CIFAR-100 setting -- the one with |Theta| = 1109240 and therefore the one where 19 extra backward passes per step actually cost something -- is never timed. The paper's efficiency claim ('spending less computation', line 596) is thus supported only where the model is a 2x100 MLP.

On CIFAR-100 the network 'has a final linear classifier per task' [lines 341-343]. That is a per-task parameter slice, so the CIFAR comparison is not a comparison of methods sharing one Theta -- it is the same confound class as EWC's per-task gains and biases in the Atari experiment [ewc Eq. 4]. It also means GEM on CIFAR requires the task descriptor at TEST time, contradicting the causal-compression paragraph's boast that GEM 'can ... be used to predict target vectors associated to previous or new tasks without making use of task descriptors' [lines 279-281], which holds only on MNIST.

FWT mostly measures dataset similarity, not method quality, and the paper does not say so. On MNIST permutations every method's FWT is within 0.0054-0.0093 of zero, because permutations destroy input-space transfer by construction ('the input distribution for each task is unrelated', line 323). On MNIST rotations the same metric reaches 0.4254 for the do-nothing 'single' baseline and 0.5524 for EWC -- neither of which has any forward-transfer mechanism at all. GEM's headline FWT of 0.6647 on rotations is therefore largely an artefact of rotations being nearly the same task twenty times over. On CIFAR-100, FWT is ~0 or negative for everyone (-0.0078 for GEM) because the classes are disjoint.

gamma is a tuned knob acting directly on the headline claim. The paper's differentiator from EWC and iCaRL is positive backward transfer; gamma is introduced with the single sentence 'we found that adding a small constant gamma >= 0 to v* biased the gradient projection to updates that favoured benefitial backwards transfer' [lines 271-272] and is then grid-searched to 0.5 -- the midpoint of the [0.0, ..., 1.0] grid, not 0 -- on all three datasets [line 805]. There is no gamma = 0 ablation anywhere, so the paper never shows how much of its positive BWT comes from the constraint mechanism and how much from this bias term.

The mechanism's guarantee is explicitly hedged and never measured. Eq. (7) is a linearisation whose validity requires local linearity and a representative memory [lines 211-213]; the paper's own conclusion is that a satisfying update is 'unlikely to increase the loss at previous tasks' [lines 224-225]. No experiment counts how often a projected step nonetheless raised a past loss, though this is directly measurable with the code that produced Pi.

Single run, no seeds, no variance. Fifteen 20-task runs are reported; not one is repeated, and no error bar, standard deviation or confidence interval appears in any figure, table or appendix. GEM's CIFAR BWT (+0.0042) and rotations BWT (+0.0048) are within a few thousandths of zero, and the paper's central qualitative claim -- that BWT is POSITIVE rather than merely near-zero -- rests on those two numbers with no dispersion estimate.

The EWC baseline is a reimplementation with two grid-searched hyperparameters (learning rate, regularization strength) and nothing else specified. The number of samples used to estimate the Fisher, whether penalties were kept per-task or merged (EWC's own unresolved fork, [ewc §2 lines 158-160]), and whether the diagonal was recomputed at every boundary are all unstated. Selected regularization strengths span three orders of magnitude across datasets (1 cifar / 3 perm / 1000 rot) [line 797], which is itself a sign of an unstable baseline.

Terminology is inconsistent within two pages: §5 splits the field into 'synaptic' memory (EWC, Zenke) versus 'episodic' memory (iCaRL, LwF) [lines 651-657], but §4.4.1 calls EWC a 'memory-based method' alongside GEM [line 614]. The monograph must not inherit this looseness -- ch07 should use the §5 split and say so.

It inherits the problem from EWC, competes with iCaRL, and looks nowhere else. The CLS citation is decorative. There is no sleep, no offline phase, no biological framing at all -- which makes GEM the corpus's cleanest demonstration that the forgetting problem can be attacked WITHOUT any of the machinery the rest of this monograph is about. systems_implications.what_changes_at_answer_time: Nothing. The deployed artifact is one weight vector (plus K linear heads on CIFAR). No retrieval, no adaptation, no extra state, identical forward pass, identical batching behaviour, identical weight sharing across users. In Rosetta terms (STC-STYLE §3): GEM is a 'model redeploy' -- (U-Theta) run once -- and everything the reader knows about serving a static checkpoint still applies.
systems_implications.what_changes_at_training_time: Per optimiser step, at round k: k-1 extra full backward passes plus a (k-1)-variable dense QP. The QP is negligible -- at most a 19x19 Gram matrix. The gradients are not: G in R^{(k-1) x |Theta|} must be materialised. This is the load-bearing systems fact and the paper's own efficiency argument sidesteps it by talking about the QP dimension instead.
systems_implications.the_scale_arithmetic_ch07_should_show: At the paper's own CIFAR scale, |Theta| = 1109240 [line 598] and k-1 = 19, so G is 21,075,560 floats = 84.3 MB in fp32 -- invisible. Carry the same construction to a 7B-parameter model in bf16 and 19 past tasks and G is 19 x 14 GB = 266 GB, plus 19 backward passes per step. THIS ARITHMETIC IS THIS NOTE'S, NOT THE PAPER'S, and must be marked as such in the text. The conclusion for the monograph: GEM's mechanism does not scale by construction, and the reason is not the QP but the requirement that all past-task gradients coexist.
systems_implications.the_obvious_degradation_the_paper_does_n: One could keep a single aggregated constraint direction instead of k-1 separate ones, reducing G to one row. The paper never mentions this, and it is exactly the move that would turn GEM into something deployable. [평가] material for ch07: the k-1-row structure is what buys per-task guarantees, and collapsing it trades the guarantee for O(|Theta|) state -- i.e. it converges toward EWC's storage profile from the other side.
systems_implications.memory_hierarchy_reading: GEM's per-step traffic is k-1 gradient reads/writes of size |Theta|, i.e. a bandwidth-bound streaming workload on top of the ordinary training step, with essentially no arithmetic intensity in the projection itself (the inner products are one pass over G). Contrast EWC, whose remembering cost is a single elementwise AXPY over |Theta| per step. Both are bandwidth-bound; GEM's constant is (k-1)x larger and grows with the round index.
systems_implications.capacity_and_privacy: GEM stores RAW user data (25.6% of the MNIST stream, 10.24% of the CIFAR stream -- F5). In any per-user or per-session deployment this is a retention liability that neither EWC nor generative replay incurs, and it is the concrete cost the E path later makes explicit and pays deliberately. ch07 should state it: the three answers to 'how does the past survive' also differ in WHAT THEY OBLIGE YOU TO KEEP ABOUT YOUR USERS.
systems_implications.what_this_paper_gives_the_serving_reader: BWT is an SLA. It is a single signed number, measurable from a matrix any serving team could already produce (evaluate the whole regression suite after each update round), that says whether the last deployment made earlier capabilities worse. Table 3 then shows the knob: more optimisation on the new round buys more regression on the old ones, monotonically, for methods without memory. That is the closest thing this corpus has to a control law for repeated Theta updates in production.
systems_implications.constraint_reminder: No memory-centric hardware argument is available from this paper and none is made here. GEM reports CPU seconds on a 2x100 MLP; NM D4's prohibition on forced connections applies.
